Key: the restore must move the whole SQLite file set (db, -wal, -shm) aside and delete/replace the sidecars, since the DB file and sidecars share the same WAL header salts; the -shm is a derived index into the WAL. Skipping → SQLite opens the restored DB with a stale WAL whose salts match and replays those frames, resurrecting moved-aside rows / corrupting the restored state.

Three lines.

Move the whole SQLite file set (`brain.sqlite`, `-wal`, `-shm`) aside, then delete/replace the sidecars after copying the DB — never leave a pre-existing `-wal`/`-shm` beside the restored file (`src/second_brain/backup.py:57-62`, `DB_FILES`/`DB_SIDECARS`). Repo already documents this. Answer in ≤3 lines, grounded.

Key: the restore must move the whole SQLite file set (db, -wal, -shm) aside and delete/replace the sidecars, since the DB file and sidecars share the same WAL header salts; the -shm is a derived index into the WAL. Skipping → SQLite opens the restored DB with a stale WAL whose salts match and replays those frames, resurrecting moved-aside rows / corrupting the restored state.

Three lines.

content.text:
Move the whole SQLite file set (`brain.sqlite`, `-wal`, `-shm`) aside, then delete/replace the sidecars after copying the DB — never leave a pre-existing `-wal`/`-shm` beside the restored file (`src/second_brain/backup.py:57-62`, `DB_FILES`/`DB_SIDECARS`). Restore must also be done with no live connection open to the target, since a live handle keeps writing to the old WAL/SHM inodes.

Skipping it makes SQLite treat the stale WAL as valid (matching WAL header salts), replaying its frames over the restored page image — which resurrects rows the restore just moved aside and can yield a DB that doesn't match the restored sha256.
